item.content:encoded:
After much thought, I've decided that the execution of the idea is internally consistent. If a system like this were used, this is how it would have to work/look.

But I just can't fit a policy of shuffling into my head-canon of the Foundation as a practical-minded paramilitary/scientific organization.

There is some security to be gained by shuffling, but they'd get the same benefit with a fraction of the effort and zero risk by having one technician write decoy articles from scratch.

YMMV, and probably does since I'm the only one griping on an article that's lasted over a year and garnered over 200 net upvotes.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I don't like the in-universe frame of a routine number shuffle.

Allow me to clarify.

The randomisation was something I put in as a means to show why there can be so many different (and contradictory) SCP-001 proposals – which, I argue, is established as part of the Foundation's lore. For all one knows, this might be one case of history alteration amped up to look as though it were more important than what it really is. I simply decide to define the special protection as a system that rewrites SCPs into 001-worthy versions (e.g. Clef's proposal might well just be a random angel guarding a thing, and not as apocalyptic as the proposal has one believe).

Second because it creates significant confusion and even danger for authorized users.

While this might be a bit harder to explain (since it is not directly addressed in the article), I see it as an extreme of how much the Foundation regards its own security. It's such that not even its own people can know the truth. It's kinda done in many other articles, using stuff like clearance levels and special authorisation. By having the very article change, it represents an extreme of the Foundation's methods.

And I guess they utilise memes or AIs to oversee the randomisation of files (and re-attach personnel during each session).

TL; DR: The bizarre measures are effectively extremes of the Foundation's security measures. After all, in this article, they so firmly believe that their course of action is correct that other alternatives are ignored.

As an aside, this was originally made for the History Contest. I wanted to make a commentary on historic events – how they can be depicted as important and yet be ignored by many as time goes by.1 Thus, I made a history-based narrative (Wrong Proposal) and then quickly shoved it in an archive of other narratives (every other article of the site). That became the randomisation.

Footnotes
1. This is coming from a guy living in a country, where STEM disciplines are highly valued at the cost of the humanities (admittedly).

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like the spin on what "consensus" really means.
It doesn't matter what the masses consider "consensus reality". It's about what those in power, the ones writing the history books (or database entries in this case) decide amongst themselves.
The minority opinion hangs a lantern on it. It would be far more reasonable to conclude that a handful of people have false memories. But this cabal prefers to believe the entire rest of humanity and all objective evidence is wrong instead. And because they happen to have the reigns of shadow government that preference is official reality.

I don't like the in-universe frame of a routine number shuffle.
First because such a measure is silly. There is no security benefit because any unauthorized person with enough insider knowledge to know they are looking for SCP-#### specifically will also likely know about the shuffle protocol and plan their hack accordingly.

Second because it creates significant confusion and even danger for authorized users. Researcher Bob has specific clearance for SCP-XXX, and only XXX. He comes in one morning to update the file with new research results, but now slot XX is a different thing he's not supposed to know about. Or a memetic hazard that he wasn't inoculated against. This is not even considering the cases where the structure of the database entry is an integral part of the containment procedures. The security risk is actually built into this story! The whole reason we are seeing these files that no one is meant to see is that the shuffle has left them momentarily exposed to anyone watching a progress monitor.

Third because it clashes with the already established framework of 001 proposals. These ultra-important files and/or red herrings are specially-protected in a secure system within a secured system. They stand apart from anything else in every way that can be arranged. If any data at all is exempt from routine procedures (and every SOP has some exceptions), it would be this seminal collection.

item.content:encoded:
This is one of the better proposals, many props for that.

A small inaccuracy I cannot help but point out. You imply that the initial O5-8 was employed by the Dutch East India Company (VOC), however, the VOC had been defunct for just over a hundred years by the time the Forbidden City Convention was ratified. By this time the former VOC territories had become part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, similar to how the British crown asserted its authority in India following the dissolution of the British East India Company.

I would suggest changing it to something along the lines of 'Special Investigations Board, Council of the (Dutch) Indies' as that was the body in charge of the Dutch colonies in the east at the time. Perhaps it helps to know that this council's exact functions and responsibilities remained somewhat unclear, with most day to day affairs being handled by the governor-general rather than the council. Seems like a good place to hide a shady precursor foundation.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If you may factor in the setup that this article is slated to no longer be 001, the weak story is there to emphasise that this is ultimately just another anomaly. Despite all the out-of-universe cries for "strong story", the SCP Foundation is fundamentally about the anomaly. Perhaps even the most basic anomalies can potentially spur the wildest extrapolations? Or perhaps this SCP is just a normal CK-class event that was deliberately spiced up to act as an 001?

And due to the SCP being a retcon of reality, one can only react to it. Hence, the O5 did what they did. For all the times fiction focuses on the people confronting Nature, people are ultimately subjects to Nature's will. Despite the initial O5's actions, they are effectively powerless against this SCP-001. It happened, no one saw it coming, and all they could do is to write about it and derive some meaning from it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm not the best at offering critical analyses, but I still have some quite shaky feelings here about this piece of work that I want to talk about. I will try my best to stay within the boundaries of the Criticism Policy.

+ An attempt at describing a man's personal (biased) thoughts
– hide block

I find the work's central narrative to be very weak. I feel like the piece did not actually tell a compelling story, or paint an interesting picture. Instead, it exists as a sort of "continuity glue" that tries to fill in the blanks of the SCP Foundation universe, focusing on building and branching off of what already exists.

The article hinges quite heavily on knowledge of the Foundation universe, its terminologies and topics. There are dozens of cross-links and references to other works to try to expand on their contents. Every section in the supplement page includes a cross-link, and every section is another attempt at expanding a topic. The problem is that while the work offered a significant amount of new insights and ideas for existing topics, none of them serve the conflict, if there even is one.

The article, in short, describes the events on which the SCP Foundation was founded, a CK-class restructuring scenario that wiped away a previous version of reality torn with anomalous conflicts, with the Foundation being founded during the Forbidden City Convention in the aftermath of the restructuring. A clear-cut origin story for the Foundation, but one without a very significant conflict, only a generic conflict of men against anomalies.

Another conflict was created (the restructuring), but was resolved with very little development (the restructuring itself was used as a device to introduce us to another world that consists mostly of expanding on the contents of other works), creating little tension. Characters were introduced (the O5 Council), but fail to actually contribute to the story, serving to expand on the universe instead. There isn't much for the reader to grip into or care about. In a way, this feels less like telling a story, and more like telling a setting for others to write on.

While there is inherently nothing wrong with developing a consistent world in which the SCP Foundation exists, the article itself felt like it was its only goal. It focuses mostly on "continuity ideas" for the reader to feel interested in. While they certainly are interesting, it doesn't justify the central weakness of the story of developing the world at the expense of having an original and meaningful conflict. The reader feels little more than just "interesting".

I am not a very experienced critic. I am merely another user on a forum on the internet. I am welcome for critiques on my opinions. I feel like I am still not seeing the whole picture here, and would like to listen to alternative opinions.

On another note, I am personally biased against crosslinks used in the way here, referring to them in text in large numbers, sometimes feeling slightly out of place.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I had to admit that the SCP 001 itself did not much for me, especially after reading all other 001s. While I appreciated the amount of research and some clever parallelism, I found it too dry and comparatively, limited in scope. However, the Addendum turned my opinion a full 180 degrees. That glimpse at the personal agendas and ruling biases of each O5 was fantastic and made me wish this was one of the first things in the site and shaped the way O5s were written ever since, showing how one's decisions are ruled by nostalgia, other's by regret or shame and so on.

I also enjoyed that the possibility that the SCP was actually the shared memories and not the alternative past, or how some believed that there were actually 12 immune and others 14, but unbeknownst to them, there were truly 13, lending credence to the "fated" argument. Now I consider SPC 001 a novel conceit to set up one of the best origin stories for the Foundation and the O5. +1

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
One point I was concerned about is the organization called "Bureau of Onmyō".

+ show block
– hide block

The simple answer is that I did not know that the Japanese site has Shushu-in. The origin of "Bureau of Onmyō" was when I was writing SCP-2478, and I want to use a prewar Japanese group. I did not know that Shushu-in was a thing, and another article in this site (SCP-2237) referred to a Japan precursor as 'Holy Emperor's Council on Unearthly Matters'.

I initially felt that the naming for the Japanese organisation in SCP-2237 to be slightly flawed, so I decided to suggest another name that would be used natively in-universe (while I explain the 'Holy Emperor's Council' away as a mistranslation). To make the new name, I look at the term 'Holy Emperor's Council' and infer that the name still suggests a group that served the Japanese Emperor. That aspect has to be retained for whatever new name I would use. In the end, I find that Heian-era bureaucrats to be a suitable choice and "Bureau of Onmyō" reflects a group of mystics under the Yamato court's control.

In short, I got the name from Wikipedia.

In reflection, I can use Shushu-in. However, I also feel that there is a need to reconcile with a tiny aspect from another pre-existing article.

P.S. MacLeod, if you are reading this, don't feel bad. Feel pride instead, for you have spurred a person's creativeness. I definitely enjoy reconciling the Holy Emperor's Council on Unearthly Matters and Bureau of Onmyō.

So, is Bureau of Onmyō a legacy of the Collection center lost in the Occult War i ? Or is it the opposite?
Or are they just the same existence with different names? Perhaps it may be just looking at a completely different parallel world.

+ show block
– hide block

In my opinion, the two groups can co-exist together. Although I do not know much of Shushu-in, my opinion is that they may have different organisations who serve different masters. Or they can serve the same master, but with different names. A parallel can be the CIA and NSA; both serve the US government but they have differences in how they do things.

As far this article is concerned, the only real difference is that the boss of Shushu-in did not retain his memory of Occult War i whereas the boss for Onmyou Bureau retained his.

As an aside, I would imagine that the Tokugawa shoguns to have an organisation to manage the paranormal. Some monasteries and shrines might have people taking care of the paranormal, who do not answer to the Emperor or Shogun. And there can be other independent investigators (which may be passed from father to son or from master to student).

In summary, I envision that before the Foundation happened, there was a more diverse and multipolar community of people dealing with the paranormal.

As a Japanese, I'm glad that you are interested in the magical history of our country.

One point I was concerned about is the organization called "Bureau of Onmyō".
As one of the GOIs famous for SCP-JP (Japanese branch) there is an organization named "蒐集院(Shushu-In) / Collective center"1. It has an old history and is regarded as a predecessor of the Foundation in some article in Japan.
So, is Bureau of Onmyō a legacy of the Collection center lost in the Occult War i ? Or is it the opposite?
Or are they just the same existence with different names? Perhaps it may be just looking at a completely different parallel world.

In any case, your article is wonderful, and it makes me feel a connection between SCP-EN and SCP-JP, and gave an opportunity to think about this mysterious relationship.

Cheers to your work!

1. Description in SCP-JP is here

Indeed. That was one of the most difficult aspects when writing this (how to showcase thirteen different people). I must thank Petrograd since he gave a strong critique on the various notes, and made me change O5-3 and O5-10's notes entirely to the versions we now see. Also, it was my PM with fuban that gave me the idea that not all precursors have to be supported by their governments or at their prime (leading to O5-10's letter).

item.content:encoded: As I got through the Description, I didn't like this for what I assumed were good reasons. And then you spent the rest of the article taking those problems and not just addressing them, but making them the central conceit of the article. You made the points I expected to make while explaining my downvote. I was blown out of the water. Great message, great writing, great work all around.

item.content:encoded:
Oh hey! This got posted! Sweet!

While there is no shortage of alternative history during this, the 2017 History Contest, I have to admire how full force this skip goes into constructing that alternate history. Where as other skips kind of tack alternate timelines on as an addition to a different effect, the effect here is the alternate timeline, which is pretty neat.

On top of that, you do a good job making the original 13 O5 members have distinct personalities and characters matching with their original organizations. Thats quite a feat, in my opinion, given the small excerpts we see from them, via their letters to their replacements.

Overall, this is both a fun addition to HisCon17 and a fun 001 proposal.

+1 MrWrong

item.content:encoded:
Fundamentally, a stupid pun (and a reference that there is no correct SCP-001 proposal).

Hmm… I will ponder a bit more on the matter.

EDIT: Okay. I thought through it. "Wrong Proposal" it be. While SCP-001 connotes a level of prestige among the SCPs, this article ultimately decides that 'SCP-001' is not objectively prestigious (and practically speaking, it is truly one article of the many).

Who could've imagined that an apostrophe can cause such a dilemma?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Besides, the collab 001 proposals don't use the apostrophe (I know mine is not a collab, but it's not like there are exceptions to the rule).

But the vast majority of proposals are single-author and use the apostrophe, making the collabs the exception.

It's ultimately your choice as an author, and there have been other exceptions, I just don't follow the logic.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is definitely fits the focus of several other SCP 001's (an SCPF origin) and while I feel it lacks some of the disquieting grandeur of proposals such as the Guardian and the Broken God, it more than makes up for it with the depth of the alternate/'actual' history, as well as the division of the O5's over how to proceed.

The rewriting of the file number itself is really humbling, and that instills a feeling of finality and catharsis I have not felt with other proposals. I do think that 'Wrong Proposal' reinforces that theme, and prefer the title sans apostrophe.

Certainly fitting for the spot. +1.
